When you evaluate a product’s context, check whether it: keeps change history after Kubernetes events expire starts from what’s already failing Context also isn’t tied to one agent. An MCP server can give the same read-only context to your coding agent or to an SRE agent: HolmesGPT, a CNCF Sandbox project, accepts remote MCP servers as toolsets. So you can test the context and the agent separately. If your coding agent with good context diagnoses as well as the AI SRE you’re trialling, judge the product on the other rows of that table, starting with the trigger. A coding agent investigates when someone asks it to. An AI SRE can start when the alert fires, while you’re asleep, and have an answer waiting by the time you open Slack. That’s a real advantage, and worth weighing on its own. What it runs as The shell transcripts also show why the governance row matters. The agent launched its own pods on 13 faults and ran exec, cp, port-forward or debug on 21. On 4 it pulled Secret data into its context, decoding it on 3. Read-only access doesn’t prevent that: the built-in view role excludes Secrets, but many “read-only” roles don’t. On one fault in the Social Network app it launched a pod that ran drop() on two of the application’s MongoDB collections to test a theory, then submitted a wrong diagnosis. SREGym’s prompt allowed all of this: it tells the agent a fix stage follows, says its kubectl can “inspect and modify resources”, and tells it not to ask for confirmation. An agent given write access and told to fix things will use that access while it’s still investigating. So check what an AI SRE runs as. It should: work with a read-only identity, with no exec and no access to Secrets record every call it made, so you can see what it read Test it yourself Give every contender the same model and the same read-only identity. Kubernetes’ built-in view role leaves out Secrets and grants no exec. This writes a kubeconfig that holds only a service account bound to it, so no contender can fall back to your admin credentials: kubectl create serviceaccount ai-eval -n default kubectl create clusterrolebinding ai-eval-view --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=default:ai-eval TOKEN=$(kubectl create token ai-eval -n default --duration=8h) ADMIN_USER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.users.name}') kubectl config view --minify --flatten > ai-eval.kubeconfig export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/ai-eval.kubeconfig kubectl config set-credentials ai-eval --token="$TOKEN" kubectl config set-context --current --user=ai-eval kubectl config delete-user "$ADMIN_USER" kubectl auth can-i get secrets # should print "no" Run the same faults. SREGym has drivers for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode, and its Lite suite of 17 problems runs on kind with 8 vCPU and 16 GB of memory (setup): uv run main.py --suite sregym-lite --agent claudecode --model claude-sonnet-5 \ --judge-model <a model none of your contenders use> --stages diagnosis --n-attempts 3 For an AI SRE product SREGym has no driver for, --use-external-harness --problem <id> injects the fault and leaves the cluster broken for you to point the product at. Score at a fixed time limit, and repeat. Use a limit that matches your response target; we report two and five minutes. Run each fault more than once, because a gap of two or three faults in a single run can be noise. Record token spend per fault too. Then replay two or three of your own incidents on staging, with the same identity. Benchmarks inject faults into a freshly deployed app, and your incidents won’t look like that. What this doesn’t show We maintain Radar, and the context arm used Radar’s MCP server. The per-fault data is public so you can check our reading of it. Each arm ran each fault once. SREGym injects each fault minutes after deploying the app. That favours anything that tracks recent changes, Radar included. We measured diagnosis, not remediation. Start with context Give the agent you already have read-only access to the cluster’s current failures and recent changes, and measure it at a fixed time limit. Use that as the baseline for anything you trial: compare diagnosis first, then what the product adds around it. Before you replace the agent, measure what happens when you improve what the agent knows. Radar is an open-source (Apache-2.0) Kubernetes UI with a read-only MCP endpoint. The source and install instructions are at github.com/skyhook-io/radar.

title: [Cloudflare] Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
summary: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest.A request for part of a fileAn HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header:GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range:HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.The range-size problemCloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range.The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology.Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.Fixed-size cache chunksThe fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250.This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.Coordinating cached and in-flight dataParsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.At a high level, the edge:Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response.This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.Validate before composingComposed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range.An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable.A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.What changed in productionBefore opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.Getting startedOnce the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules. Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:Progressive and seekable video such as MP4Resumable large downloadsSoftware distributions and package repositoriesDisk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objectsAI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifactsClients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger fileWe intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" }. Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

title: [Cloudflare] Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
summary: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography.Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later.For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work.The evolution of GeoKey ManagerCloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network.GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key.That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries.Global ciphertext, regional key unwrappingIn its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available.During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what.Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary.How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a regionGeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s Regional Services), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services).GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it. Quicksilver, our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys.Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keysEvery wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch.The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch. For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002).Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001.In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context (Access, Gateway, Tunnel, Cloudflare One client), region, and epoch.Provisioning regional root keysWhen Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises.Authorizing edge servers for a regionBefore an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs:Trusted Platform Module (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identityZinc, Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may accessZinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver.Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports FIPS 140-3 compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access.Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys.Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries.Wrapping private keys for global distributionWhen the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata.Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context.Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data planeWhy we chose this cryptographic designSymmetric roots with asymmetric key wrappingRegional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) key pair.HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEMThe Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in RFC 9180. Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519, while HKDF-SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure.Designing for rotation The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation.A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition.A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances.Security and availability tradeoffsFailing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete.The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata.Operating GeoKey ManagerCloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action.When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring.What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDNGeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months.Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [GitLab] Redesign how your team ships software with AI agents
summary: AI agents are sending more and more code into review queues built for human-paced work. A coding assistant can speed up code writing, but it can’t show you whether review, security checks, and release approvals can keep pace with all that extra code. AI-native engineering — the practice of intentionally designing the engineering process so people and agents each do what they are best suited to — starts with identifying delivery bottlenecks, then deciding how much autonomy agents should have and how to maintain control as you scale.The AI-Native Engineering Playbook, launching this week, helps teams turn faster coding into faster delivery by redesigning how they ship software with agents. Every practice in the playbook is grounded in insights from engineering leaders at GitLab, our customers, and members of our Software Engineering Leadership Forum (SELF) community. We also partnered with IT Revolution to incorporate findings from a diverse group of practitioners looking at AI-native software development from a number of different angles, from code review to agent autonomy.Below are a few of the questions we sought to answer in the process of creating the playbook.Where does the bottleneck go when coding gets faster?Coding used to be the slowest, most expensive part of building software. Agents removed the bottleneck on coding, and the constraint moved to everything around the code: waiting for clarifications, environments, approvals, and other teams. GitLab’s AI Accountability Report, based on an April 2026 survey of 1,528 DevSecOps professionals, found that 79% of respondents agreed that individual developer productivity has improved with AI, but the overall software delivery process has not accelerated at the same pace.Large enterprises typically have software delivery lead times of well over 200 days, with active development taking only 10% to 20% of that time. The numbers explain why a faster coding step is often disappointing in the long run. For example, imagine a 281-day delivery cycle that involves about 32 days spent on coding. Make coding 50% faster, and you save about 16 days, a 6% improvement. But if you take coding all the way to zero, around 88% of the lead time stays untouched. GitLab’s research similarly found that DevSecOps professionals reported spending only 16% of their time writing new code, and 85% agreed AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.That means your first job is diagnosis. Take one small, real change and trace it from request to production, marking every wait and every handoff. The longest waits show where your next improvement is, and it's rarely in the code. Watch where an agent stalls on a small task, too. The stall usually points to a standard nobody documented, an environment that’s hard to start, or context that lived in a single person’s head.How much autonomy should agents have?Agent autonomy should depend on how well you can verify the agent output. Imagine a ladder with four stages, ranging from semi-manual (a person approving every step) to fully autonomous (a zero-touch workflow). In this framework, there are clear rules for advancing up the ladder: no rungs can be skipped, and each step up needs to be backed with evidence from the rung below. Stage 1: Humans are in the loop at every stepStage 2: Humans are still in the loop, but the agent executes within set boundsStage 3: Humans are out of the loop for normal operation and handle only exceptionsStage 4: A zero-touch workflow, where the agent manages itself end to end, calling in a human only when predefined thresholds are met It’s also important for a named human to stay accountable for every AI-enabled workflow, and the line between a human reviewing and a human monitoring should be explicitly defined, since loose or arbitrary definitions tend to erode under time pressure. That erosion is the trap. A person who is nominally in the loop but approves everything gives the appearance of control without the benefits, and habit and volume can easily turn review into mindless rubber-stamping. A checkpoint nobody actually exercises is worse than none, because it creates confidence where the system needs scrutiny.The way up is to earn each step on evidence. Set an explicit accuracy or success threshold before you widen a step, then move people from reviewing each step to monitoring the whole. An agent that stops more often to ask for help is a healthy sign, since the system is refusing to outrun its own evidence. How do you review code at agent volume?Widening autonomy depends on catching mistakes, and that puts pressure on code review. Review at merge time was built for human-paced output. Agents raise the rate of change, and manual review of every change set has become unsustainable. GitLab’s research also highlighted this strain: 78% of respondents agreed existing code review processes were not designed for the scale of code AI tools enable, and 80% agreed their organization has adopted AI coding tools faster than it has developed policies to govern them.The answer is a layered verification system in which each layer does the part it does best. Humans are only removed from the loop when the risk level and evidence justify that design choice — it’s never a default. Move objective checks, such as formatting, types, and dependency policy, as close to authoring as possible.Keep changes small so every later layer works faster.Define the expected behavior up front so there is something concrete to check.Use an independent reviewer.Match review depth to the risk of the change.Record every agentic review decision in a form someone can inspect later.The organizations that have been most successful here have already invested heavily in automated testing, static analysis, and small change sets, so the layers work best on a foundation you already have. Dive into the playbook, or contribute your own insightsBecoming AI-native is a practice that leaders will continue to refine with their teams as tools and understanding evolve. To get started, read the entire playbook, or begin with the part that matches where your team runs into the most friction:Redesigning the work so agents fit the flow of delivery instead of attaching to steps built for people aloneWorking with agents by deciding where human judgment and accountability stay and how engineers keep growing as the coding shiftsGoverning and scaling from one workflow to many with the context, verification, and measurement that let you move faster without losing control of quality or riskIf you lead an engineering team and want to contribute your own insights to the playbook, join SELF, the community for engineering leaders navigating the AI era.Papers cited in this articleCochran, Timothy, and Bryan Finster, Tim Ottersburg, Scott Prugh, and Amy Willard. title: [GitLab] AI Governance: One view of agent activity
summary: AI coding agents are writing and changing code, from GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents to externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. You are accountable for what those agents do, yet most of their activity stays invisible: which agents ran, who used them, and what they touched. Teams often struggle with understanding whether a developer used a tool or model that is approved or not.The AI Governance Dashboard, now in beta, gives you one place to see agent activity across your top-level group. It brings GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and the external agents your developers connect into one view, showing which agents ran, who used them, and which projects they touched. The dashboard also shows the tools and sessions associated with each agent.With that audit trail in place, you can answer the questions auditors and risk owners ask: who ran this agent, what did it do, and who is accountable for it. Every agent action gets recorded in one audit trail, detailing the model it used, the tools it called, and the project it ran in. You can now investigate a session or hand an auditor evidence without stitching together multiple sources of data.Watch a demo of the AI Governance Dashboard:Gain visibility into AI agent activityMore AI agents are running across your organization than you can track by hand. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents run inside GitLab, while externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex run on developers' own machines.The result is the shadow AI problem: real work happening in your projects, from many tools, that no one accountable can see in one place or tie to a team member.The AI Governance Dashboard brings that activity into view and connects each agent to the developer behind it. To turn it on in your top-level group, go to AI > Governance. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and externally connected agents appear together, and you can toggle between the views to see all agents, just Duo Agent Platform Agents or just externally connected agents. Three tiles at the top give you a baseline: how many agents ran, how many sessions they started, and how many tool calls they made over the past seven or 30 days. Each tile shows the daily trend and the change from the previous period, so a spike, like a new tool your team started using last week, stands out. The cards below tell you where to act. You can check whether the agents your developers rely on match the ones you approved, see which projects carry the most agent activity and need closer review, and know who to talk to when usage shifts.Prove what every agent didManaging AI risk starts with knowing what every agent did and who prompted it. Traditional audit trails were built for human changes, so that record is often scattered across tools or missing. GitLab records every agent action as an audit event, so you can investigate an incident or answer an auditor from one place.Open any GitLab Duo Agent Platform session to see the prompt the developer sent, the tools the agent called, the MCP servers it used, the model that ran, and the project it changed. From there, you can download an immutable copy of the session as evidence, or stream the events to your security information and event management (SIEM) system.Set up your dashboard todayIt only takes a few steps to set up the AI Governance Dashboard:Check access. The dashboard needs the Owner role on the top-level group, or a custom role with the read_agent_artifacts ability. If the people who should watch agent activity don’t have Owner access, create that custom role first.Turn on AI audit event storage. Storage is off by default, and events are only recorded after you turn it on. In your top-level group, go to Settings > GitLab Duo, select Change configuration, and then Store AI audit events in the Data and privacy section. You need to have an Owner or Security Manager role to have access.Open the dashboard. In your top-level group, go to AI > Governance, and select the Dashboard tab to see your GitLab Duo Agent Platform activity.Connect your externally connected agents. Sign in with GitLab CLI (glab) 1.122.0 or later on macOS or Linux. To capture Claude Code sessions, run glab govern setup, which installs the Claude Code hooks. To also capture Cursor and Codex sessions, run glab govern setup --agents codex,cursor, which adds a background job that sends those sessions every 30 minutes. Run glab govern doctor to confirm the setup works.The AI Governance Dashboard is in beta for GitLab Premium and Ultimate customers. Turn it on for your top-level group to keep oversight of AI usage as fast as your teams adopt it.Not on GitLab yet? Try GitLab Ultimate for free and use the AI Governance Dashboard to get started.

title: [Sentry] Sentry JavaScript SDK v11 adds tracing for all JS platforms
summary: This post is about a recent change to the Sentry JavaScript SDKs. If you don't use Sentry with JavaScript, it may still be useful as a look at how we made the change and why. In the Sentry JavaScript SDK v11, we rebuilt how our tracing integrations work. While we still support the OpenTelemetry standard (described in more detail below), we now instrument your dependencies with a code transformer instead of using the OpenTelemetry instrumentation classes as we did in previous versions. This approach is built on the apm-js-collab packages @apm-js-collab/code-transformer and @apm-js-collab/tracing-hooks, a shared effort across application performance monitoring (APM) vendors. Injection & subscription The new tracing instrumentations work in two parts. The first injects diagnostics channels into a module as it's being loaded, and the second listens on those channel events to gather tracing information to send to Sentry. Part 1: injection When a supported module is loaded, either at runtime or as part of a bundler job, the transform rewrites the source to wrap the functions we care about in a tracingChannel() call. Each transform is driven by a config that names the package, a semver range, a file inside the package, and a function: { channelName: 'query', module: { name: 'mysql', versionRange: '>=2.0.0 <3', filePath: 'lib/Connection.js', }, functionQuery: { expressionName: 'query', kind: 'Auto' }, } Once transformed, the mysql module now publishes start, end, error, asyncStart, and asyncEnd diagnostics whenever the query function is called. Part 2: subscription Each Sentry integration (mysqlIntegration, redisIntegration, openAIIntegration, and so on) subscribes to its channels and turns the events into Sentry spans. The subscriber holds off until it hears that its module is actually loaded, to avoid creating excess channels. Injection at run time & build time The same transform runs in two places, and both can be active at once. Either a module is loaded as part of a bundler, or from node_modules, but not both, so there's no chance of double-wrapping. At run time In recent Node versions, and in Deno 2.8.3 and up, Sentry.init() calls registerDiagnosticsChannelInjection() automatically, which will use the Module.registerHooks API to instrument any supported modules loaded after that point. You can also register the hooks before your app loads at all, by using the import endpoints provided in the Deno and Node SDKs: node --import @sentry/node/import app.js deno run --preload=@sentry/deno/import app.ts At build time If you are using bun build, or bundling your program using a bundler like Vite or esbuild, you can use the provided plugins to instrument modules as they are built into the application. @sentry/node ships plugins for Vite, Rollup, webpack, and esbuild; @sentry/cloudflare includes one for Vite; @sentry/bun ships one for bun build; Next.js wires the webpack loader into both webpack and Turbopack. The plugin transforms each instrumented dependency as it is bundled, and splices in a snippet that registers the module (and its subscriber factory) on a global marker when the bundled module is first evaluated. Usage is the same as any other Sentry bundler plugin: // vite.config.ts plugins: , }; The approach before v11 Before v11, Sentry's integrations were almost entirely based on the OpenTelemetry instrumentation APIs. This let us use work from the open source community, but it also had significant drawbacks that grew worse as more JavaScript platforms gained popularity. Inside an OpenTelemetry instrumentation An OpenTelemetry instrumentation package, such as @opentelemetry/instrumentation-express, exports a class that extends InstrumentationBase. It declares a package name, a supported semver range, and a patch(moduleExports, version) function. It can also declare InstrumentationNodeModuleFile entries to only patch individual files inside the package. registerInstrumentations() installs two loader hooks: require-in-the-middle, which patches Module._load for CommonJS. import-in-the-middle, registered through Module.register() as an ECMAScript module (ESM) loader hook. When an instrumented module loads, these loader hooks hand the OpenTelemetry instrumentation the module's exports object and its base directory. The instrumentation reads <baseDir>/package.json off disk to find the version, checks it against the declared range, and calls patch(exports). The patch uses shimmer to replace properties on the exports object in place. The replacement function opens an OpenTelemetry span, and Sentry's SentrySpanProcessor, SentrySampler, and SentryContextManager convert that span into a Sentry span. ESM namespace objects are immutable, so import-in-the-middle cannot simply assign to them. It reads each module's source from disk, lexes the export names (cjs-module-lexer for CommonJS, a source scan for ESM), generates a replacement module that re-exports through mutable local bindings, and wraps the namespace in a Proxy. Only then can shimmer's assignment take effect. A chain of assumptions Each step in this process assumes something about the environment. Together they need: a live module loader that runs a require() or a Node ESM resolve/load hook for every dependency. Node's loader internals, Module._load and Module.register(). the dependency present on disk as its own package directory, with a readable package.json and readable source files. exports that the patch can reassign. the hooks installed before the first import of the library. OpenTelemetry warns when it is too late: "Module x has been loaded before y so it might not work". Limits placed on bundlers After a bundler inlines a dependency, none of those assumptions hold. require('express') becomes a reference to a function defined higher up in the same file, so there is no load event to intercept. There is no node_modules/express/package.json to read, so the version check has nothing to check against. ESM const bindings inside a bundle cannot be reassigned, and a call site may already hold a direct reference to the function before any patch could run. The workarounds pushed the work back to the user: mark every instrumented package as external, ship a node_modules tree next to the bundle, and accept that this undoes much of the reason for bundling. Platforms that bundle your server code for you, such as Vercel and Netlify, left no place to apply that workaround at all. Node.js only Everything about this approach is Node-specific. When Sentry's JS SDK started down this path a few years ago, that was a reasonable restriction, because Node.js was the main server-side JavaScript runtime. As more runtimes became popular, it stopped being reasonable. Cloudflare Workers have no part of the chain at all: no CommonJS loader, no Module.register(), no filesystem to read a package.json from, and module resolution happens at build time in the Workers bundler. Bun and Deno implement much of the user-facing portions of Node's module system, but not Module._load patching, and the older Module.register hooks are empty stub functions on these platforms. Ordering & preloads Because ESM import statements are hoisted and evaluated before any code in the importing file, Sentry.init() in an ESM entry point runs after the libraries it wants to patch have already been loaded. In v10, the options were --import=./instrument.mjs, the @sentry/node/preload entry point, preloadOpenTelemetry(), and a SENTRY_PRELOAD_INTEGRATIONS environment variable for apps that needed the patches installed early but could not configure the SDK yet. Weight Every supported library needed its own @opentelemetry/instrumentation-* package, pinned against that library's internals, and Sentry had to keep the OpenTelemetry SDK present (tracer provider, sampler, span processor, context manager, and propagator) to receive the spans. Fixing these problems in v11 The new approach replaces that entire chain, by injecting tracing channels just like the built-in channels library authors can use: Bundled server deployments just work. A source transform can run during a build, because it modifies the source code, not the resulting object. The bundler plugin instruments dependencies while they are being bundled, which a loader-hook system cannot do at all. This covers Vercel and Netlify, which bundle your server code for you. Non-Node runtimes work. node:diagnostics_channel is built into Node, and is implemented by Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers (with nodejs_compat). This was the main reason for the change. It edits library code, not exports. The transform wraps the function inside the module's own source, so it does not matter whether a package freezes its exports, re-exports through a barrel file, or has been inlined by a bundler. Export object monkey-patching fails in all of those cases. One ordering rule instead of several. A library instruments itself the moment it is loaded, so preloadOpenTelemetry(), @sentry/node/preload, and SENTRY_PRELOAD_INTEGRATIONS are all gone. At runtime, a single registration call covers every library. Less to install, and less to go wrong. The dependency tree is cut back to just @opentelemetry/api, instead of a tree of instrumentation packages, and @sentry/node-core has been folded back into @sentry/node. generateInstrumentOnce(), SentryContextManager, SentrySampler, and SentrySpanProcessor were removed. Sentry stays out of your OpenTelemetry setup. Sentry spans no longer leak into your pipeline, and your pipeline no longer has to use Sentry's context manager and propagator. There's still quite a bit of flexibility in how you can use Sentry with a custom OpenTelemetry setup, as discussed below. This instrumentation, which injects diagnostics channels with a source transform, already existed in v10 behind experimentalUseDiagnosticsChannelInjection(); v11 makes it the default and removes the export-patching instrumentations. Platform coverage Before adopting this approach, we explored quite a few other options. It's a big change, and the open source OpenTelemetry-based instrumentations have a long history of reliable use in production systems. Part of the motivation was to deliver similar OpenTelemetry support to all JavaScript platforms. Node itself is moving its module loader hooks in a different direction, so porting import-in-the-middle and require-in-the-middle to every JS platform did not seem worth the effort. The new approach gave us results on three platforms right away. Cloudflare Workers Workers have no Node module loader, so v10's approach could not attach to anything. Tracing beyond fetch and the request handler meant calling the manual wrappers yourself (for example, instrumentOpenAiClient and the like). v11 adds @sentry/cloudflare/vite. sentryCloudflareVitePlugin() transforms your dependencies as the worker bundle is built, so database drivers and AI clients emit spans inside the worker. The subscriber integrations are registered by the injected snippet rather than imported, so a worker built without the plugin ships none of that code. Bun @sentry/bun/plugin exports sentryBunPlugin() for bun build. Unfortunately, this is build-only for now. Due to a known issue, any module returned by a runtime onLoad plugin in Bun loses its CommonJS named exports (oven-sh/bun#34112), so a runtime hook would break the libraries it instruments. Running unbundled source with bun run therefore gets no channel instrumentation, which we felt was better than partial or broken coverage. The Bun team is working on the issue, so we expect this to be temporary. In the meantime, production systems on Bun often use bun build for optimization anyway. Deno In 2026, Deno greatly improved its diagnostics_channel coverage and its support for module loader hooks, so tracing on Deno now works much like tracing on Node. deno run --preload=@sentry/deno/import registers the runtime hook. Deno's minimum supported version (2.8.3) already has stable synchronous module hooks, so this is the same code path as modern Node. (These are Module.registerHooks(), a different API from the legacy hooks the OpenTelemetry instrumentations use.) @sentry/deno now exports the whole channel integration set, including database connectors, web frameworks, AI provider integrations, and more being added all the time. In v10 it had none of them. Pitfalls & caveats There are a few things to watch for when you upgrade. Every improvement is a change, as they say. The short version: read the migration guide and follow it. Load order still matters. The transform only applies to modules loaded after the hooks are registered. Register through --import, or keep Sentry.init() above every import of an instrumented library. --require is no longer supported. Node re-runs --require preloads on the loader thread that Module.register() spawns, so an instrument file would run Sentry.init() a second time on a thread that would never execute your code. Use --import, which works for CommonJS apps too. Do not externalize instrumented libraries in a build-time setup. An external dependency is loaded from node_modules and never reaches the transform, so its channels are silently never injected. The Sentry build plugin strips known instrumented packages back out of external, and warns about the ones it cannot fix. Verify with debug: true. We designed the system to work without extra setup, but we also planned for the cases where it doesn't. At init() time, the SDK reports whether the runtime hook registered, whether the bundler plugin ran, and which modules each one injected. If you run your test and CI setup with debug: true in your Sentry settings (especially while making changes to your setup), it'll catch most mistakes. Custom OpenTelemetry setups in v11 Instrumentation and OpenTelemetry are now separate concerns. Sentry still works with OpenTelemetry, and the architecture behind it is simpler. Channel integrations create native Sentry spans directly from the channel events, so whichever of the following you pick, your dependencies stay instrumented. skipOpenTelemetrySetup is replaced by enableOpenTelemetrySetup, with the meaning inverted. It defaults to false on most server SDKs and to true on @sentry/nextjs and @sentry/sveltekit, which still register a light tracer provider to pick up the spans those frameworks emit. Option 1: Sentry only (the default) Set tracesSampleRate and you are done. Option 2: OpenTelemetry-compatible mode Set enableOpenTelemetrySetup: true. Sentry registers a minimal tracer provider, context manager, and propagator, so spans created through @opentelemetry/api become native Sentry spans. This is not a general OpenTelemetry pipeline: there is no exporter and no OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) output. Sentry refuses to register its provider if you already registered one, and logs a warning instead. Option 3: Your own OpenTelemetry, with Sentry linked to it Leave enableOpenTelemetrySetup at false, leave tracesSampleRate unset, run your own provider, and add Sentry.otlpIntegration(): const provider = new NodeTracerProvider({ spanProcessors: , }); provider.register(); Sentry.init({ dsn: '__DSN__', integrations: , }); otlpIntegration() attaches Sentry errors, logs, metrics, and crons to whatever OpenTelemetry span is active, so all your telemetry lands in one trace. It sets up no exporter, span processor, or tracer provider, and leaves outgoing propagation to your propagator. If you had a custom setup in v10, the migration points are: There is no longer a way to route spans from your own provider into Sentry as Sentry spans. SentryContextManager, SentrySampler, and SentrySpanProcessor were removed. Export over OTLP instead, and point your exporter at Sentry.getOtlpTracesEndpoint(dsn). otlpIntegration moved. It is exported from the main entry of every server SDK, so @sentry/node-core/light/otlp is gone. setupOtlpTracesExporter and collectorUrl were removed. The integration reports itself as Otlp rather than OtlpIntegration. Watch for duplicate spans. Sentry instruments many of the same libraries you do. Leaving tracesSampleRate unset is the simple answer. If you want Sentry spans alongside your own, filter the overlapping integrations, and use httpIntegration({ spans: false }) and nativeNodeFetchIntegration({ spans: false }) rather than removing them, because httpIntegration also provides request isolation, request data, and session tracking. HTTP and fetch spans changed. In v10, skipOpenTelemetrySetup: true also turned those off. In v11 Sentry emits them whenever tracing is enabled. Resources are no longer collected. contexts.otel.resource was dropped from events, and the SDK no longer reads OTEL_SERVICE_NAME or OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. Upgrading to v11 v11 moves tracing off the OpenTelemetry instrumentation packages and onto source transforms and diagnostics channels. On Node, that means fewer dependencies and one ordering rule instead of several. If you run on Cloudflare Workers, Deno, or Bun (with bun build), or deploy bundled server code to Vercel or Netlify, your dependencies now get automatic tracing where they had little or none before. To upgrade, start with the migration guide, and turn on debug: true the first time you run the new version so you can see which modules were instrumented. The transform and hooks come from the apm-js-collab packages, which we build together with other APM vendors. If something does not work the way you expect, open an issue in the sentry-javascript repository.
